level1.text: On an air track a $0.40\,\text{kg}$ cart moves to the right at $0.50\,\text{m/s}$ and a $0.25\,\text{kg}$ cart to the left at $0.60\,\text{m/s}$. What is the total momentum of the carts when right is the positive direction? Give the momentum with its sign.

On an air track a $0.50\,\text{kg}$ cart moves at $0.80\,\text{m/s}$ and collides with a $0.30\,\text{kg}$ cart at rest. The carts stick together. Friction is neglected. At what velocity do the carts move on together?

Two skaters stand facing each other at rest on ice and push each other. The masses of the skaters are $60\,\text{kg}$ and $45\,\text{kg}$. After the push the lighter skater glides at $1.2\,\text{m/s}$. The friction of the ice is neglected for the duration of the push. At what velocity does the heavier skater glide?

On an air hockey table puck A, of mass $0.16\,\text{kg}$, slides at $4.0\,\text{m/s}$ and hits puck B, of mass $0.20\,\text{kg}$, at rest head-on. After the collision puck A slides back in the direction it came from at $0.44\,\text{m/s}$. Friction is neglected. What is the velocity of puck B after the collision?

Two similar $0.30\,\text{kg}$ carts move towards each other on an air track: one to the right at $0.60\,\text{m/s}$ and the other to the left at $0.20\,\text{m/s}$. The carts collide and stick together. Friction is neglected. At what velocity do the carts move on together?
Two air-track carts collide and stick together. External forces are negligible during the collision. Which statement about this perfectly inelastic collision is correct?
level1.answer: Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy decreases, because some of it changes into internal energy.

choices.text: Kinetic energy is conserved, but the total momentum decreases, because the carts slow down in the collision.
choices.feedback: Momentum is conserved when the impulse of the external forces is negligibly small. Kinetic energy is the quantity that decreases in a perfectly inelastic collision.

choices.text: Both momentum and kinetic energy decrease, because the objects stick together.
choices.feedback: Sticking together does not remove momentum: the common momentum of the carts is the same as before the collision. Only kinetic energy decreases.

choices.text: Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy decreases, because some of it changes into internal energy.
choices.feedback: Correct: internal forces do not change the total momentum, so it is conserved. Some of the kinetic energy changes into internal energy and sound in the deformations.

choices.text: The total momentum is conserved and kinetic energy increases, because the combined mass of the carts is greater.
choices.feedback: Kinetic energy cannot increase without a source of energy. The common velocity becomes smaller so that $\tfrac12 mv^2$ after the collision is smaller than before.

level1.text: A skater of mass $35\,\text{kg}$ stands at rest on ice and throws a $2.0\,\text{kg}$ ball horizontally at $6.0\,\text{m/s}$ relative to the ice. Friction is neglected for the duration of the throw. At what velocity does the skater glide after the throw? Give the magnitude of the velocity.

In billiards a $0.17\,\text{kg}$ cue ball moves at $1.8\,\text{m/s}$ and hits an identical ball at rest head-on. The collision is elastic and friction is neglected. What is the velocity of the ball that was hit after the collision?

level2.text: A $0.50\,\text{g}$ bullet is fired from an air rifle at $180\,\text{m/s}$. The mass of the rifle is $3.2\,\text{kg}$, and before the shot it is at rest, lightly supported by the shooter. The support of the shooter is neglected for the short time of the shot. At what velocity does the rifle start to move backwards?

An ice hockey player of mass $85\,\text{kg}$ glides at $6.0\,\text{m/s}$ and checks a $75\,\text{kg}$ player who is standing still. After the collision the players glide on together. The friction of the ice is neglected for the duration of the collision. How much of the players' kinetic energy changes into other forms of energy in the collision?

On an air track a $0.20\,\text{kg}$ cart moves at $0.60\,\text{m/s}$ and collides with a $0.40\,\text{kg}$ cart at rest. After the collision the lighter cart moves back in the direction it came from at $0.10\,\text{m/s}$. Friction is neglected. What percentage of the original kinetic energy of the carts remains after the collision?

In a rail yard a $30\,000\,\text{kg}$ freight car moves at $1.8\,\text{m/s}$ and collides with a car at rest. The cars couple together and move on together at $1.2\,\text{m/s}$. Rolling resistance is neglected for the duration of the coupling. What is the mass of the car that was at rest?

On an air track cart A ($m_\text{A} = 0.50\,\text{kg}$) moves to the right and collides with cart B ($m_\text{B} = 0.30\,\text{kg}$) at rest. The collision was carried out in three different ways, and the velocities were measured with video analysis. Right is the positive direction, friction is neglected and the data is example data.

a) Calculate the total momentum before and after in each experiment. Is momentum conserved within the measurement accuracy?

b) Calculate the kinetic energy before and after in experiments 1 and 2 and classify the collisions as elastic, perfectly inelastic or partially elastic.

c) Calculate the fraction of the original kinetic energy that remains in experiment 3 and classify the collision.

The answer box takes the fraction of part c) as a percentage.

level2.text:
On an air track cart A ($0.40\,\text{kg}$) moves to the right and collides with cart B ($0.60\,\text{kg}$) at rest. The positions $x$ of the carts were measured with video analysis (example data). The collision takes place at about $2.0\,\text{s}$, and the carts move at constant velocity before and after it. Friction is neglected.

a) Determine the velocities of the carts before and after the collision from the table.

b) Is the total momentum conserved within the measurement accuracy?

c) What percentage of the original kinetic energy remains after the collision?

The answer box takes the result of part c).

A student solves a problem: on an air track a $0.60\,\text{kg}$ cart moves to the right at $0.80\,\text{m/s}$ and a $0.20\,\text{kg}$ cart to the left at $0.40\,\text{m/s}$. The carts collide and stick together. Friction is neglected.

The student's solution: $v' = \dfrac{0.60 \cdot 0.80 + 0.20 \cdot 0.40}{0.60 + 0.20}\,\text{m/s} = 0.70\,\text{m/s}$.

What is the error in the solution? Calculate the correct common velocity with its sign, when right is the positive direction.

The answer box takes the correct common velocity.

level3.text:
The velocity of a bullet is measured with a ballistic pendulum: a $2.0\,\text{kg}$ block of wood hangs at rest from a long string, and a $10\,\text{g}$ bullet is fired horizontally into the block at $400\,\text{m/s}$ and stays in it.

The bullet stops in the block so quickly that the block does not have time to move during it. After that the block and the bullet swing up together. Air resistance is neglected.

How high does the block rise from its lowest point? Answer in centimetres.

A firework rocket of mass $0.90\,\text{kg}$ rises straight up at $12\,\text{m/s}$ when it explodes into two pieces. The $0.30\,\text{kg}$ piece continues straight up at $40\,\text{m/s}$, and the other piece moves vertically.

The impulse of the weight and of air resistance is neglected for the short time of the explosion.

What is the velocity of the other piece immediately after the explosion? Give the velocity with its sign when upwards is the positive direction.

An astronaut is on a spacewalk, at rest relative to the space station, $12.0\,\text{m}$ from the station, when the safety tether comes loose. The mass of the astronaut with the spacesuit is $120\,\text{kg}$. The astronaut throws a $3.0\,\text{kg}$ tool away from the station at $4.0\,\text{m/s}$ relative to the station. How long does it take for the astronaut to drift back to the station?

Investigators are studying an accident in which car A hit a parked car B, at rest, from behind on a straight horizontal road. Example situation: the mass of A is $1100\,\text{kg}$ and the mass of B is $1400\,\text{kg}$. The cars stuck together and slid on together $8.0\,\text{m}$ to a stop, according to the skid marks. All the wheels were locked, and the coefficient of sliding friction of dry asphalt is $\mu = 0.60$.

Assume that friction and air resistance can be neglected during the collision itself and that during the sliding only a constant sliding friction acts on the cars.

a) Calculate the common velocity of the cars immediately after the collision using the work–energy principle.

b) Calculate the velocity of car A before the collision.

c) The driver of car A claims to have been driving at the speed limit of $50\,\text{km/h}$. Is the claim consistent with the result? How does the uncertainty of the friction coefficient $\mu = 0.50 \dots 0.70$ affect the conclusion?

The answer box takes the result of part b) in $\text{km/h}$.

Students study the effect of friction on a collision. Cart A ($0.40\,\text{kg}$) slides on a level table and hits cart B ($0.20\,\text{kg}$) at rest, to which it attaches with a strip of hook-and-loop tape. A light gate measured the velocity of cart A just before the collision as $1.50\,\text{m/s}$. The velocity $v$ of the pair of carts sliding together was measured with video analysis (table, example data), and the time $t$ is counted from the moment of the collision.

Using the first measurement point, a student calculated the total momentum after the collision and concluded that momentum is not conserved. Assume that friction is a constant force caused by the table and that its impulse is negligibly small during the collision itself.

a) Determine the magnitude of the deceleration of the pair of carts from the table.

b) Calculate the friction force that slows the pair of carts.

c) Deduce from the table the velocity of the pair of carts immediately after the collision and check the conservation of momentum. What was wrong in the student's reasoning?

The answer box takes the friction force of part b).
